questions.stem: Month-end, three issues in one firm: (a) the audit manager's sibling is the client's new finance controller who prepared the estimates being audited; (b) a client pays 45% of the firm's total fees, and renewal talk is 'friendly but clear'; (c) the client's owner offers to fund the partner's family wedding with an 'old friendship' gesture; and the firm also proposed implementing the same client's accounting software last quarter.

o: Self-interest through fee dependence — evaluate magnitude and client's significance; safeguards (EQR, disclosure to those charged with governance of the client, fee structure) and if dependence is severe and long-term, decline/withdraw over time
Ignore percentages — no bright line exists
questions.why: 45% of total firm fees from one client is a textbook economic-dependence threat with no safe harbour percentage; the framework evaluates the RITP test and lists safeguards; if the dependence can't be diluted or managed, the direction is to lose the dependence (fee restructuring) or the client.

o: Refuse — a RITP would see it as compromising objectivity and the gift's value/timing makes self-interest/intimidation acute; firm policies on gifts typically cap or forbid
questions.why: Gifts from a client to a covered person's family, timed during the audit, are the 'no' list, not the disclosure list — trivial-and-insignificant is the only pass, and a wedding gift from an audited owner is neither.

questions.q: Issue (d) the software proposal — now that they are the auditor:
o: Prohibited for an audit client: the firm implementing the accounting system creates a self-review threat into the records it audits; decline, or only provide it where the entity's own governance genuinely takes responsibility and the standard permits, otherwise the independence is gone
Only for software the auditor won't see
questions.why: Designing/implementing the financial reporting system for an audit client is self-review at the root of the records — the answer in most jurisdictions for a listed audit client: no; for unlisted entities with strong governance, a narrow advisory-only version may pass with safeguards — the exam answer states the threat by name and the default refusal.

questions.q: If, after all, the client threatens to replace the firm unless the FY-end estimates are signed off 'as filed':
o: Undue influence/intimidation: document, do not change the technical position; report to TCWG, consider the professional obligation to record, and where independence/objectivity can't be sustained — resign (with the statutory/other reporting duties)
questions.why: Threat of replacement tied to accepting management's position is the INTIMIDATION limb; the framework's safeguard set is governance-level (audit committee awareness) plus the professional's final step: the position does not move for fear of losing the fee — and the withdrawal route exists where it would.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the five fundamental principles of the ICAI Code of Ethics / IESBA?
questions.why: The five: Integrity, Objectivity, Professional competence and due care, Confidentiality, Professional behaviour; SKEPTICISM is a mindset duty inside competence/objectivity (SAs), NOT a Code principle — the confusion is the trap.

mem.tip: A principle is a vow; a mindset is a habit.

questions.q: An audit partner holds a small financial interest in the audit client. This creates which threat under the conceptual framework?
questions.why: Financial interests → SELF-INTEREST; auditing your own work → self-review; promoting the client's position (e.g. defending a treatment publicly) → advocacy; long-close relationship → familiarity; pressure from management to reduce scope → undue influence/intimidation.

questions.q: A member accepts an audit assignment with remuneration contingent on the client securing a bank sanction. This is:
o: A self-interest threat — and professional-act conduct violation for an assurance engagement; contingent basis for audits and specified work is prohibited
Permissible for statutory audit if disclosed
An integrity threat but permitted by the board
questions.why: Code/First-Schedule conduct: contingent-fee arrangements for assurance (audit, review, certification) create unacceptable self-interest and are prohibited; other engagements with evaluation — safeguards; the fee must not depend on the outcome the member is certifying or facilitating.
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — outcome-linked pay for a certifier = buying your own judgment AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Never pay the referee by the goals.
mem.link: Chapter 19 — Professional Ethics & Liabilities of Auditors

questions.q: A client offers the audit partner an all-expenses family holiday at a resort they audit for hospitality pricing: the partner should:
o: Refuse where a reasonable and informed third party would conclude objectivity is compromised; nominal hospitality, if any, with firm-level policies
Disclose in the audit file and accept
questions.why: Conceptual framework test: the 'reasonable and informed third party' (RITP) benchmark — if it fails, reject; trivial-and-insignificant is the threshold; self-interest/intimidation; disclosure does not cure it, it is a safeguard for a lower-grade threat.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — the RITP test: a stranger's eyes decide Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Sunshine cures small things; not this kind.
mem.link: Chapter 19 — Professional Ethics & Liabilities of Auditors

questions.q: An auditor's professional confidentiality is properly overridden when:
o: There is a legal or professional duty to disclose (e.g. statutory fraud reporting) or specific client permission
Any third party sues for information
A regulator requests without authority — if the 'request' comes by phone
questions.why: Disclosure permitted where there is a legal/professional duty (143(12) fraud reporting path, court orders, ICAI/peer/NFRA inspections) or client consent — the fourth option's 'phone request without authority' fails the verification test: a right to demand is not the same as the one asked by.

questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — duty-to-disclose and right-to-with-disclose are different gates AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Secrets must be safe, not silent when the law speaks.

questions.q: Hospitality from an audit client may be accepted when:

questions.why: The test is not the approval chain — trivial-and-insignificant under the reasonable-informed-third-party lens, with firm policy caps.

questions.why: Key audit partner rotation and cooling periods attack familiarity/self-review; family relationships trigger removal from the engagement — the safeguard is distance, not disclosure.

questions.q: For a listed audit client, providing book-keeping or systems design is:
o: Generally prohibited — it is self-review into the very records/controls being audited
questions.why: Assurance and creation can't mix: preparing the records the audit tests is the self-review threat the framework bars at the listed level.

questions.topic: Rotation of audit firms — listed companies
questions.q: The audit-firm rotation regime for listed companies under the framework:
o: Maximum continuous engagement terms (3 years, with an eligibility break) — the independence safeguard by expiry, driving the SAs' transition procedures (opening balances, predecessor communication)
questions.why: DOCUMENTED statutory design (Companies Act + rules): firm-term caps and cooling periods make rotation a planned handover, not an accident — with the 510-style opening-balance obligations at every rotation year.
questions.trend: Traceable to a real, publicly-notified amendment/standard (documented fact), tested in ICAI style.
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — rotation is an opening-balance event AI prediction, not a certainty.

questions.q: After mandatory rotation of a key audit partner, the framework typically imposes:
o: A cooling period during which the former partner may not rejoin the engagement (nor advise on it, in the listed-company regime)
A lifetime ban from the firm
questions.why: Rotation + time-out is the familiarity/self-interest antidote: the partner's judgment on the area they owned for years doesn't age out with the title, so the standard ages the person out for a while.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — distance needs duration AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Leave the table; don't hover at the same seat.

questions.q: An audit firm acting for the client before a tax tribunal raises which threat, and the framework's usual answer?
o: Advocacy — prohibited for the audit client (listed) where the position becomes adverse; safeguards/decline
questions.why: Speaking FOR the client while grading their statements is advocacy — the framework bars it in the listed regime (or requires safeguards and independence evaluation where permitted at all): the auditor cannot be both witness and mouthpiece.
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — advocacy is the profession's clearest red line AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: A referee doesn't argue for the team.
mem.link: Chapter 19 — Professional Ethics & Liabilities of Auditors

questions.q: A member who solicits clients by advertising or circulars breaches the Code because:
o: Professional rules on publicity restrict direct solicitation/advertising (beyond the permitted identity circulars and website disclosure norms) to protect objectivity and the profession's standing
questions.why: The advertising regime is India-specific: broad publicity is restricted (name, address, qualifications, services and fee structures only within rules), and active solicitation is professional misconduct — the contrast with most IESBA jurisdictions is exam gold.
questions.trend: Traceable to a real, publicly-notified amendment/standard (documented fact), tested in ICAI style.
questions.probWhy: HIGH likelihood for Nov 2026 — publicity has a permitted list, solicitation has none Prediction is study guidance, not an ICAI statement.

mem.tip: A chartered accountant markets with restraint — by rule, not by taste.
